\chapter{Saying It Is Not So}
\label{ch:mr-sentence-negation}
\hlchaptermodality{32}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can negate a whole Marathi sentence, say that I do not know, and decline an offer with nako rather than nahii.}

Complete MR-R32-not-so and produce all three unaided: I do not like milk, I do not know, and no thank you.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[… nāhī]{… \mr{नाही} — saying that a whole sentence is not so}

\label{lesson:MR-C32-nahi-verb}



\begin{quote}
Retrieve the two things the last chapter did with \textbf{\mr{ना}}: the doubled front pair, and the tag on the end. Then say the full word \textbf{\mr{नाही}} on its own, the way you have said it since the courtesy chapter — as an \textbf{answer}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: \mr{नाही} at the end of a sentence, not instead of one}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{मला} \mr{दूध} \mr{आवडत} \mr{नाही}.} — \emph{malā dūdh āvaḍat nāhī.} — \textbf{I don't like milk.}
\end{quote}

Until now \textbf{\mr{नाही}} was a whole reply. Here it is a piece of a sentence, and the rule is short:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the verb drops back to its bare \textbf{-\mr{अत}} shape — \textbf{\mr{आवडते}} becomes \textbf{\mr{आवडत}}
  \item \textbf{\mr{नाही}} follows it, at the very end, carrying the whole denial
\end{itemize}

Marathi does not slip a \emph{not} in front of the verb the way English does. It finishes the sentence and then cancels it. That order is worth saying out loud a few times, because it is the opposite of the English habit and it is what a listening paper's distractors are made of: \emph{āvaḍtaṁ} and \emph{āvaḍat nāhī} differ only in what comes after.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{मला} \mr{माहीत} \mr{नाही}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{मला} \mr{माहीत} \mr{नाही}.} — \emph{malā māhīt nāhī.} — \textbf{I don't know.}
\end{quote}

You have had \textbf{\mr{मला} \mr{माहीत} \mr{आहे}} for a long time. Swap \textbf{\mr{आहे}} for \textbf{\mr{नाही}} and you have the single most useful sentence a beginner owns: the honest admission that lets a conversation continue instead of stopping.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{malā chahā āvaḍto} then \emph{malā dūdh āvaḍat nāhī}
  \item \emph{malā māhīt āhe} then \emph{malā māhīt nāhī}
  \item where the denial sits in Marathi — \textbf{at the end, after the verb}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where does \textbf{\mr{नाही}} go when it denies a whole sentence? (\textbf{At the end, after the verb}.) What happens to \textbf{\mr{आवडते}} in front of it? (\textbf{It drops back to \mr{आवडत}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nako]{\mr{नको} (nako) — \textquotedblleft{}no, thank you\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:MR-C32-nako}



\begin{quote}
You can now accept with \textbf{\mr{चालेल}} and deny a fact with \textbf{\mr{नाही}}. Between them sits a gap: how do you turn down something you are being \textbf{offered}?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{नको}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{नको}} — \emph{nako} — \textbf{no thank you; I don't want it}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{चहा}? — \mr{नको}, \mr{धन्यवाद}.} — \emph{chahā? — nako, dhanyavād.} — \textbf{Tea? — No thank you.}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\mr{नाही}} says a thing is not so. \textbf{\mr{नको}} says you do not want it. Answer an offer with \textbf{\mr{नाही}} and you have said something slightly odd — that the tea does not exist. Marathi keeps the two apart, and so should you.

The word carries the same ancient \textbf{na-} as \textbf{\mr{नाही}}, with an old \emph{be wanted} verb worn into its second syllable. That history is exactly its meaning: \textbf{\mr{नको}} is \emph{let it not be wanted}, which is why it can refuse an offer and can never answer a question of fact.

Its polite partner is the one you already have. \textbf{\mr{चालेल}} accepts, \textbf{\mr{नको}} declines, and \textbf{\mr{धन्यवाद}} goes on the end of either.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{chahā? — chālel}
  \item \emph{dūdh? — nako, dhanyavād}
  \item which of \emph{nāhī} and \emph{nako} answers an OFFER — \emph{nako}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which word declines an offer? (\textbf{\mr{नको}}.) Which one says a thing is not so? (\textbf{\mr{नाही}}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%A8\%E0\%A4\%95\%E0\%A5\%8B}{Wiktionary: \mr{नको}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nāhī · nako]{Four ways of saying no}

\label{lesson:MR-R32-not-so}



\begin{quote}
You now hold four different noes: the answer \textbf{\mr{नाही}}, the doubled \textbf{\mr{ना} … \mr{ना}}, the sentence-final \textbf{\mr{नाही}}, and \textbf{\mr{नको}}. Only one of them can refuse a cup of tea.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{malā chahā āvaḍto paṇ dūdh āvaḍat nāhī} — the joining word and the denial in one sentence
  \item \emph{malā māhīt nāhī}
  \item \emph{nako, dhanyavād}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which no goes at the END of a sentence and cancels it? (\textbf{\mr{नाही}}.) Which one answers an offer? (\textbf{\mr{नको}}.) Then stop.
\end{tcolorbox}
